SupeRR Selector Season 2 · Round 1

Under Pressure

Who keeps their level when the chase gets tight, and who falls away. Prepared by Arush Sharma.

The short version

Pressure here means the state of the chase, not one moment in it. The side needs 10 or more runs an over with six or fewer wickets down, or 12 or more an over in the last 18 balls. Each player is compared with his or her own normal level, not with the league average.

      Where pressure sits

      Across all matches, pressure covers 40% of chase deliveries, and between 37% and 44% in each season. It gets heavier as the chase goes on: the last three overs are where it piles up.

      How we measured it

      Everything here comes from the supplied ball-by-ball file. The problem statement left the pressure definition and the score to us, so we say exactly what we used and why.

      The data

      • ball_by_ball.csv: 200,961 deliveries across 867 matches with ball data (first and second innings; 38 super-over deliveries are excluded).
      • matches.csv (883 matches listed): revised overs and revised target. competitions.csv: format and season.
      • The problem statement sets the task and the submission rules. It gives no score formula, so the formulas below are ours.

      What counts as pressure

      Only the chase counts. A ball is under pressure when either rule holds before it is bowled.

      Rule A: required run rate ≥ 10 AND wickets lost ≤ 6 Rule B: balls remaining ≤ 18 AND required run rate ≥ 12 Required run rate = (target − runs so far) × 6 ÷ legal balls left Target = revised target where present, else first-innings total + 1

      Batting score

      How much faster a batter scores under pressure than normally, with more credit for more pressure balls faced.

      Gain = pressure strike rate − normal strike rate (normal = all other balls, wides excluded) Weight = pressure balls ÷ (pressure balls + 100) Score = Gain × Weight Eligible: at least 150 balls faced and 60 pressure balls

      Bowling score

      How much less a bowler concedes and how many more wickets they take under pressure, with the same weight as batters.

      Economy drop = normal economy − pressure economy (runs per over) Wicket gain = pressure wickets per over − normal wickets per over Score = (Economy drop + 20 × Wicket gain) × Weight Eligible: at least 300 legal balls and 60 pressure balls

      How reliable it is

      • Each player's matches are resampled 1,000 times (seed 20261110), and the ranks are recalculated each time. The 90% rank range and the top-10 share come from those resamples.
      • Split-half check: scores in 2022–24 are compared with 2025–26, by rank correlation, for players with 30 or more pressure balls in both halves. Batters ρ = (n = ), bowlers ρ = (n = ). A value near 0 means the halves barely agree.
      • Sensitivity (all matches): batter top-10 overlap is when the 100 in the weight is changed to 50 or 200. Bowler overlap is when the wicket value of 20 is changed to 0, 10 or 30. With both pressure rules at 12 or more, the overlap is .

      Limits and assumptions

      • No control for the opposition, the venue, or the batter against bowler matchup.
      • Byes and leg-byes are not recorded per ball, so each counts as 1 run towards the target.
      • The 2026 season is partial in the supplied data.
      • Earlier version: the 21,831 pressure balls (22.9%) in the earlier deck do not reproduce from the stated definition, which gives 38,530 (40.5%). The earlier script is not in the folder. This version replaces the earlier top-10 lists.
